A young bride waited in Room 501 of a grand beach hotel for a ship that never came, and guests say she is still watching the Gulf from the turret.
Galveston, Texas. The Hotel Galvez on Seawall Boulevard, opened in 1911.

The Galvez went up on the new seawall a decade after the 1900 hurricane killed about 6,000 people in Galveston, and it became the island's grand beachfront address. Gamblers, movie stars and presidents stayed there, and during World War II the Coast Guard took it over. Since the 1950s, guests have reported ghosts, especially on the fifth floor.

The best known is Audra, the "Lovelorn Lady." The story says that in the mid 1950s a young bride to be checked into Room 501 to wait for her fiancé, a sailor, and climbed to the hotel's west turret every day to watch for his ship. After a storm she was told it had gone down with all hands, and in her grief she hanged herself in the turret. Days later, the legend says, he arrived in Galveston alive. Guests in 501 describe doors slamming, lights and TVs switching on, phones ringing with no one on the line, key cards that will not work, and a woman crying near the fifth floor elevators.

The debate: no record has ever been found that confirms who Audra was or that she died there, and the hotel runs its own ghost tours. Historians call her folklore. Guests who stayed in 501 are not so sure.

Would you book Room 501?

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hotel_Galvez

For five months, thousands of people across Belgium said a giant black triangle was floating silently over their towns, and one night the Air Force sent two F-16 fighters after it.
Eupen, Belgium. November 29, 1989 to April 1990.

Top 5 things to know about the Belgian UFO wave:

1) Where it started: the first big night was November 29, 1989, around Eupen, near the German border. 143 people reported seeing something, and by the end of the wave thousands claimed sightings.

2) The shape: most witnesses described a large, flat triangle flying low and slow with bright lights underneath, often with no sound at all.

3) The scramble: on the night of March 30, 1990, ground radar tracked an unknown target and two Belgian Air Force F-16s were sent up to find it. The pilots never saw it with their own eyes, but the Air Force released a report on the night, and the case is still argued over today.

4) The photo: in April 1990 a picture of a black triangle with lights at its corners, taken near Petit-Rechain, went around the world. Experts could not prove it fake for 20 years. In 2011, the photographer admitted it was a polystyrene model with lightbulbs.

5) The explanations: skeptics point to helicopters, media hype and the fact that many reports came in after the news coverage. Belgium's air staff suspected secret American stealth planes, but the U.S. said none were flying there.

Which is stranger: thousands of witnesses, or radar that saw what the pilots couldn't?

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgian_UFO_wave

A Homeland Security patrol plane's heat camera locked onto something racing across an airport in the dark, and then it dove into the ocean and came back out as two.
Aguadilla, Puerto Rico. Rafael Hernández Airport, the old Ramey Air Force Base, about 9:22 PM, April 25, 2013.

A U.S. Customs and Border Protection Dash 8 patrol plane was flying near the airport when its infrared camera picked up a small, warm object with no lights. The crew kept the camera on it for about three minutes as it crossed the runway area, skimmed low over houses and trees, and headed out over the beach. Then it appeared to plunge into the Atlantic, come back up, and split into two objects before the footage ended.

In 2015, a team from the Scientific Coalition for UAP Studies went through the video frame by frame and said the object flew below treetop level at up to about 100 mph through an urban area without hitting anything, then entered the water with almost no splash.

The debate: in March 2025 the Pentagon's UFO office, AARO, closed the case. It said the objects were most likely a pair of sky lanterns drifting on the wind, which hotels near the beach often release, and that the "dive" was just the lanterns cooling until the camera could no longer see them. Researchers still argue about the speed and the split.

Sky lanterns, or something that can fly into the sea and come back out?

Source: https://www.dvidshub.net/video/944204/puerto-rico-objects

Police officers in five small Illinois towns watched the same huge lighted object glide over them before dawn, and one of them ran to his trunk for a camera.
Lebanon, Illinois. St. Clair County, east of St. Louis, about 4:10 AM, January 5, 2000.

It started when a man walked into the Highland police station and asked an officer to come outside and look at something hovering in the sky. The call went out over the county radio. In Lebanon, Officer Ed Barton looked southeast and saw two extremely bright white lights hanging in the sky, part of a much larger dark shape. Officers in Shiloh, Millstadt and Dupo heard the traffic and went looking too. In Millstadt, Officer Craig Stevens watched it pass at about 4:28, grabbed the Polaroid from his squad car's trunk, and got one blurry picture in the 15 degree cold before it slipped away to the northwest.

Witnesses described something as big as a football field, flat or triangular, with bright white lights and red lights at the rear, moving slowly and silently, then speeding off. Its path ran about two miles from Scott Air Force Base, which said it had no aircraft like that in the air and did not track anything on radar.

The debate: the officers' descriptions do not match perfectly, and skeptics say lights seen at night from different angles are easy to misjudge. But five officers in five towns were on the radio about the same thing at the same time.

If five officers saw it, why does nobody know what it was?

Source: http://www.ufoevidence.org/cases/case277.htm

The man who would design the U-2 and SR-71 spy planes watched a black saucer hang over the Pacific for three minutes, while his own test pilots chased it at 17,000 feet.
Agoura, California. A hilltop ranch three miles west of Agoura, about 5:00 PM, December 16, 1953.

Clarence "Kelly" Johnson, chief engineer at Lockheed, was watching the sunset through his ranch house window when he noticed a dark object above the mountains to the west. He thought it was a smoke trail or a lenticular cloud, but its sharp outline never changed and it did not move for at least three minutes. He sent his wife for the binoculars, ran outside, and watched the long, thin ellipse speed off to the west in a shallow climb. Within 90 seconds it was gone. He placed it roughly over Point Mugu.

At the same time, a Lockheed crew was flying a Navy Super Constellation test flight off the coast. Test pilot Roy Wimmer called out "Look out, there's a flying saucer," and co-pilot Rudy Thoren turned straight toward a dark, sharp edged object that looked like a giant flying wing. They flew at it for about five minutes at some 225 mph and never gained on it. Then it shrank to a speck and vanished, heading west. The next morning, before Thoren could say where or when, Johnson told him.

The debate: Project Blue Book filed it as a lenticular cloud. Johnson wrote that he was "more firmly convinced than ever" such craft exist, and an Air Force general noted he had been reluctant to write the report at all. The Pentagon released the full file on November 20, 2026.

If the best aircraft designer of his era couldn't explain it, who could?

Source: https://www.newsnationnow.com/space/ufo/eight-uap-radar-analysis-object-mach-2-5/

For 168 years this prison held killers, bank robbers and a future heavyweight champion, and the guides who lead night tours there now say some of the prisoners never left.
Jefferson City, Missouri. The Missouri State Penitentiary on the bluffs of the Missouri River, opened in 1836 and closed in 2004.

When it shut down, it was the oldest operating prison west of the Mississippi. Sonny Liston learned to box inside its walls, Pretty Boy Floyd and Emma Goldman did time there, and in 1967 James Earl Ray escaped hidden in a bread box on a delivery truck, a year before he killed Martin Luther King Jr. A riot in 1954 left four inmates dead, dozens hurt and buildings burned, and from 1938 to 1965 the state put 39 people to death in the small stone gas chamber that still stands on the grounds.

Since the prison opened for tours, guides and guests have described footsteps on empty walkways, cell doors moving on their own, shadow figures in the old 1868 A-Hall, and voices in the underground dungeon cells. Guides tell visitors that blondes and redheads are the ones most likely to be touched, and some guests say it happened to them. Ghost Hunters and Ghost Adventures have both filmed there.

The debate: the site sells ghost tours by the night, so the stories are good for business, and an old stone cellblock full of drafts, echoes and steel doors will always sound like someone is walking right behind you.

Would you sign up for the five hour ghost tour?

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_State_Penitentiary

A radio telescope in Ohio caught a signal from deep space so strong that the volunteer reading the printout circled it in red and wrote one word in the margin: "Wow!"
Delaware, Ohio. Ohio State University's Big Ear radio telescope, 10:16 PM Eastern, August 15, 1977.

Top 5 things to know about the Wow! signal:

1) The telescope: Big Ear was a huge open air radio telescope near Perkins Observatory in Delaware, Ohio, and from 1973 it ran the longest search for alien radio signals in history.

2) The note: a few days after the signal hit, volunteer astronomer Jerry Ehman was going through the computer printouts when he saw the string 6EQUJ5, circled it and wrote "Wow!" beside it. Those characters measure how loud the signal was over time. They are not a coded message.

3) The channel: it came from the direction of the constellation Sagittarius, very close to 1420 megahertz, the natural radio frequency of hydrogen. Back in 1959 two physicists had picked that frequency as the most likely channel an alien civilization would use to call.

4) Seventy two seconds: as the Earth turned, Big Ear could watch one point in the sky for about 72 seconds, and the signal rose and fell across that whole window, just like something fixed out in space. The telescope had two receiver horns, and the signal should have shown up in the second one about three minutes later. It never did.

5) It never came back: Ehman and later teams pointed telescopes at that patch of sky more than 100 times. Nothing. Explanations include an Earth signal bouncing off space junk, hydrogen around passing comets, and a natural flare from a cloud of hydrogen gas. None has been confirmed.

If it was a message, why did it only knock once?

Learn more: https://www.bigear.org/wow.htm

A farm wife walking home from feeding her rabbits saw a silver disc gliding silently over the field, and her husband grabbed the camera and took two of the most famous UFO photos ever made.
McMinnville, Oregon. The Trent farm near Sheridan, about 13 miles southwest of McMinnville, about 7:30 PM, May 11, 1950.

Evelyn Trent called to her husband Paul, who ran for the family's loaded Kodak and snapped two pictures of the slow, metallic, disc shaped object before it sped off to the west. Paul's father said he saw it too. The Trents later said they thought it might be a secret military plane and worried the pictures would bring trouble, so they did not rush to show anyone. A local banker put the prints in his window, the McMinnville Telephone-Register ran them on the front page on June 8, and Life magazine printed them weeks later.

In 1967, astronomer William K. Hartmann of the Air Force funded Condon Committee studied the negatives and interviewed the Trents. He wrote that this was one of the few UFO reports where everything he checked appeared consistent with an extraordinary, silvery, metallic, disc shaped flying object, tens of meters across. He also admitted it could be a small model hanging from a wire.

The debate: skeptics Philip Klass and Robert Sheaffer called it a hoax, pointing to shadows that look like morning rather than evening and a shape that resembles an old car mirror. In 2013 a French research group said it could see a thread above the object. Evelyn and Paul Trent insisted it was real until they died in the 1990s, and McMinnville now throws one of the biggest UFO festivals in the country every spring.

Do those two photos show a real craft or a model on a string?

Source: https://www.nicap.org/500511mcminnville_dir.htm

A glowing object shaped like a mushroom hovered over a Kansas sheep farm, and when it shot away it left a glowing ring on the ground that went numb under a woman's fingers.
Delphos, Kansas. The Johnson family farm in Ottawa County, about 7 PM, November 2, 1971.

Sixteen year old Ronald Johnson was doing chores near the sheep pen with the farm dog, Snowball, when he heard a rumble like a washing machine out of balance. About 75 feet away, an object shaped like a toadstool, about 8 feet across, hung 2 to 5 feet above the ground with a shimmering glow running from its base down to the dirt. When it tilted and shot away with a high whine like a jet, Ronald was briefly blinded. His parents, Durel and Erma, ran outside in time to see a light in the sky and a glowing ring on the ground. When Erma touched it, her fingertips went numb.

The next day, reporter Thaddia Smith of the Delphos Republican called the Ottawa County Sheriff. Undersheriff Harlan Enlow found a doughnut shaped ring of bone dry soil in a yard that was otherwise mud, with broken limbs on the trees nearby. They had to force Snowball back to the spot, where he shivered and pawed the ground. Weeks later, investigator Ted Phillips found the soil in the ring still dry about a foot down and the ring outlined in snow that would not melt.

The debate: doubters have blamed a fungus ring or a hoax, but the sheriff's office saw the ring the next day and the family told the same story for the rest of their lives.

What could leave a ring of soil that water would not soak into?

Source: https://www.nicap.org/ar-711102rep.htm

Two airline pilots watched eight glowing red discs race in under their plane and flip around in a hairpin turn "like balls bouncing off a wall."
Norfolk, Virginia. Over the Chesapeake Bay, 20 to 25 miles north of Norfolk, 9:12 PM, July 14, 1952.

Pan American First Officer William B. Nash and Second Officer William H. Fortenberry were flying a DC-4 airliner at 8,000 feet on a clear night when they saw a red glow on the ground ahead, near Newport News. It turned into six round, flat objects shaped like coins, each about 100 feet across, glowing a fiery red and flying in a tight line about 2,000 feet above the bay. Almost directly under the airliner, all six stopped short and reversed direction in a sharp 150 degree turn. Two more, brighter than the rest, came up from behind the plane and joined them. Then all eight blinked out together, lit back up, and climbed as a group toward Newport News before winking out one by one.

The debate: ground witnesses reported similar lights that night, the Air Force questioned both pilots, and Project Blue Book filed the case as an unknown. Later skeptics blamed ground lights seen through haze, fireflies trapped between the cockpit window panes, and even a mirage of the planet Venus.

Could two veteran airline pilots really mistake fireflies for eight discs?

Source: https://www.nicap.org/520714norfolk_dir.htm

The carrier that brought Apollo 11 home from the moon is a museum now, and the people who work aboard say some of its old crew still walk the passageways.
Alameda, California. The USS Hornet (CV-12), docked at Alameda Point on San Francisco Bay, a museum ship since 1998.

The Hornet fought across the Pacific in World War II, served off Vietnam, and in July 1969 hauled Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins out of the ocean after the first moon landing. Almost as soon as she opened to the public in Alameda, staff and volunteers started reporting footsteps and voices when nobody else was aboard, sailors and officers in uniform who disappear around a corner, radios and lights switching on by themselves, and phantom cigar and cigarette smoke. The Admiral's cabin and the engine rooms get the most stories, and the ship now runs paranormal overnights where guests sleep in the old crew bunks.

The debate: the ghost stories rest on two numbers that get repeated everywhere, more than 300 men dead aboard over 27 years of service and the highest suicide rate in the Navy. Ghost shows and tour sites repeat them, but none of them point to a Navy casualty record behind those figures. Skeptics say an old steel ship full of pipes, cables and hatches will groan and bang all night, and a museum that sells ghost tours has every reason to keep the stories going.

Would you spend a night in one of those bunks?

Source: https://www.kqed.org/news/12011685/the-uss-hornet-in-alameda-is-a-destination-for-paranormal-enthusiasts-and-you-can-spend-the-night-there

A fighter pilot locked his radar on a blazing light over Iran and tried to fire a missile at it, and at that exact moment his weapons panel went dead.
Tehran, Iran. The sky over the capital and Mehrabad Airport, the night of September 18 to 19, 1976.

Top 5 things to know about the 1976 Tehran UFO incident:

1) The calls: around 11 PM, people in Tehran started phoning the Mehrabad Airport tower about a bright object hovering over the city. The tower supervisor stepped outside, saw it himself and called the Imperial Iranian Air Force.

2) The first jet: at 1:30 AM an F-4 Phantom took off to intercept. About 25 nautical miles out, it lost all its instruments and radio. When the pilot turned back, everything came back on.

3) The radar lock: a second F-4 locked onto the object on radar at 27 miles, a return the size of a 707 tanker, flashing blue, green, red and orange so fast the crew could not see its body. A smaller light shot out of it straight at the jet. When the pilot, later named as Parviz Jafari, tried to fire a Sidewinder missile, his weapons control panel and radios died, and he dove away.

4) Something landed: another light dropped out of the big one and settled on the ground, lighting up an area two to three kilometers wide. In daylight a helicopter crew found nothing on the dry lake bed, but picked up a strange beeper signal near a small house.

5) The paper trail: a U.S. defense attache report went to the Defense Intelligence Agency, the White House, the CIA and the National Security Agency, and the DIA review called it "an outstanding report" and a classic case. Skeptics say the bright light was the planet Jupiter and the failures were the F-4's known electrical problems.

Equipment failure, or something that switched them off?

A police officer radioed in that a silent boomerang of lights as big as a football field was hovering right over her patrol car.
New Castle, New York, in the Hudson Valley. Cross Ridge Road near the Taconic State Parkway, about 9 PM, March 24, 1983.

Officer Andi Sadoff was parked on patrol when another officer came over the radio asking for backup because he was watching something incredible. She grabbed the mic: "Unit 5 to base, I see it too, it's hovering above my car. I'm following it." For about eight minutes she trailed a huge V of white and green lights until it slipped behind the hills. That night, police from Carmel to Yorktown were swamped with calls, a UFO hotline logged more than 300 reports, and drivers stopped on the Taconic to watch something they called a floating city glide over the trees at walking speed.

It was not a one night thing. People across Westchester, Putnam and Dutchess counties reported the same silent boomerang for years, and many of the witnesses were police officers on patrol.

The debate: state police traced the lights to a group of pilots flying small planes out of Stormville Airport in tight formation, with dark painted undersides and bright lights they could switch off all at once. The pilots called themselves the Martians. Sadoff and many others said they saw one solid object hovering in total silence, which small planes cannot do.

Could a few small planes fool a cop parked right underneath them?

Source: https://www.nytimes.com/1984/08/25/nyregion/strange-sights-brighten-the-night-skies-upstate.html

An egg shaped object with a single white light came down over the runways of a nuclear weapons base, and then radar watched it fall in behind a military plane.
Albuquerque, New Mexico. Kirtland Air Force Base, about 10:45 PM, November 4, 1957, the night after Sputnik 2 went up.

Two civilian control tower operators, R.M. Kaser and E.G. Brink, saw a lighted object come down steeply at the east end of the runway. It left the flight line and crossed the runways and taxiways at less than 100 feet, heading toward the tower. Through binoculars it had no wings, no tail and no fuselage, just an egg shape standing on end, 15 to 20 feet tall, "the size of an automobile standing on its nose," with one white light at its base. It hovered near a restricted area for about a minute, then climbed steeply into the overcast.

The tower called the base radar unit. Radar showed a target heading east, then turning south at very high speed toward the Albuquerque radio range station, where it circled for several minutes. Then it came back toward Kirtland and took up a position right behind an Air Force C-46 that had just taken off, and stayed there until both left radar range.

The debate: the Air Force and later the Condon Report decided it was a small, powerful private plane with no flight plan whose lost pilot tried to land at the wrong airport, then pulled up when he saw the lit restricted area. The radar operator said the return looked like a normal aircraft. Both tower men said it looked nothing like a plane.

Would a lost pilot really hover over a nuclear base?

Source: https://www.nicap.org/ncp/ncp-kirtland57.htm

An Army radar locked onto something too fast for the set to follow, and 25 minutes later two Air Force pilots dove after a silver disc.
Point Pleasant, New Jersey. The Army Signal Corps radar school at Fort Monmouth and the sky over Sandy Hook, 11:10 AM, September 10, 1951.

A student operator was demonstrating an AN/MPG-1 radar for a group of visiting officers. When he switched to automatic tracking, he picked up a low target moving along the coast so fast the set could not keep up, about 700 miles per hour. He had to follow it by hand until it was gone.

At 11:35 AM, Lt. Wilbert Rogers and Major Ballard were flying a T-33 jet trainer at 20,000 feet over Point Pleasant when Rogers saw a dull silver, flat, disc shaped object far below, 30 to 50 feet across, heading toward Sandy Hook. He nosed down and banked after it. The object banked too, showing its round flat edge, then turned out to sea and pulled away even as he pushed the jet to 550 mph. The next day, radar sets at the fort tracked more fast targets that nobody could name, and the reports landed at the Pentagon.

The debate: the Air Force investigators blamed the radar track on a student's mistake and the pilots' disc on two weather balloons released that morning from the Evans Signal Laboratory nearby. The pilots said the thing banked, turned and outran a jet, which is not something a balloon does.

Could a balloon outrun a jet?

Source: https://www.nicap.org/reports/monmouth.htm

The bullet holes in the walls are real. The 26 people said to have died inside have never been named, and the ghosts keep showing up anyway.
Tombstone, Arizona. The Bird Cage Theatre on Allen Street, opened December 24, 1881, now a museum.

The Bird Cage was a theater, saloon, gambling hall and brothel in a silver boom town, and the legend says it never closed, running day and night for eight years. Curtained boxes hung over the gambling floor, and the New York Times supposedly called it the wildest, wickedest night spot between Basin Street and the Barbary Coast. When the mines flooded and the boom died, it was shut up for decades with much of its furniture still inside.

The ghost stories go back to at least the 1920s, when students at a school across the street said they heard laughter and music from the locked, empty building and smelled cigar smoke. Staff and visitors today describe women in period dresses, men in cowboy hats, unseen hands that push, and a man in black striped pants and a visor who walks across the stage carrying a clipboard. TV ghost hunting crews have called it one of the most haunted buildings in the West.

The debate: the 120 to 140 bullet holes are real, and anyone can count them. The death toll is another story. No source names the 26 dead or dates their deaths, the famous New York Times line has never been matched to an actual issue, and an 1894 newspaper's tale of a twelve dead shootout in the boxes is set a year before the Bird Cage even opened.

Would you stay after closing to count the bullet holes?

Source: https://thehauntedstates.com/is-the-bird-cage-theatre-haunted/

A night fighter locked its guns on a radar target over England, and then the target got behind him and followed him through every turn.
Lakenheath, England. RAF Lakenheath and RAF Bentwaters in Suffolk, both U.S. Air Force bases, the night of August 13 to 14, 1956.

Top 5 things to know about the Lakenheath-Bentwaters UFO case:

1) The 4,000 mph blip: radar at Bentwaters tracked a target about 30 miles east moving at 2,000 to 4,000 mph. It disappeared two miles east of the station and showed up three miles west of it. Bentwaters then called Lakenheath with a question: "Do you have any targets on your scopes traveling at 4,000 mph?"

2) Stop and go: at the Lakenheath radar center in Suffolk, watch supervisor T/Sgt. Forrest Perkins and his crew watched objects travel, stop dead and then move off again at high speed with no visible acceleration. People on the ground reported round white lights.

3) The tail chase: the Royal Air Force scrambled a de Havilland Venom night fighter. The pilot called it "the clearest target I have ever seen on radar" and radioed that his guns were locked on. Then the target moved behind him. Perkins said it stayed on the jet's tail for about 10 minutes while the pilot tried everything to shake it, and sounded "pretty scared."

4) The verdict: the Air Force funded Condon Report studied it as Case 2 and concluded that "the probability that at least one genuine UFO was involved appears to be fairly high." For a report that explained away almost everything else, that line still stands out.

5) The twist: decades later, British researchers David Clarke, Andy Roberts, Martin Shough and Jenny Randles found the Venom crews. They said the radar contacts were unimpressive, there was no tail chase and nobody saw anything. "All we saw was a blip which rather indicated a stationary target," one navigator said. Skeptics also point to radar anomalies and Perseid meteors.

The radar logs or the aircrews, who do you believe?

A man called 911 and told the dispatcher two beings, 8 to 10 feet tall with big shiny eyes, were standing in his backyard looking at him.
Las Vegas, Nevada. A home in the northwest valley, just after midnight on May 1, 2023.

At about 11:50 PM on April 30, a Las Vegas Metro officer's body camera recorded a bright light streaking low across the sky. People from eastern California to Utah reported the same fireball. Roughly 40 minutes later, a man called 911. He said he, his father and his brother were working on a truck in the yard when something bright fell, they felt a big impact and heard footsteps. "I swear to God this is not a joke," he told the dispatcher. "They're 100% not human."

Officers arrived about half an hour later. "I have butterflies, bro," one said on the drive over. A family member told him it was a big creature, more than 10 feet tall, and the officer admitted another cop had seen something fall out of the sky too. When he walked into the backyard, police blacked out the video, citing privacy laws. Drone video later showed a circular imprint in the dirt.

The debate: NASA's planetary defense officer said the fireball was a small meteor, high up and hundreds of miles away, so nothing from it landed in anyone's yard. Skeptics point out that only two brothers said they saw the figures. Police closed the case. But a false 911 report is a felony in Nevada, and the family has stood by its story.

If you saw what they saw, would you have called 911?

A ball of light with no plane behind it turned and came head on at a fighter pilot over Fargo, and four other people watched it happen.
Fargo, North Dakota. Hector Airport, about 9 PM, October 1, 1948.

Lt. George F. Gorman of the North Dakota Air National Guard stayed up in his F-51 Mustang to log some night flying after the rest of his squadron landed. The tower cleared him in and warned him about one Piper Cub nearby. Then a blinking light passed him on the right, and the tower said there was no other traffic. He went after it. The light was six to eight inches across, perfectly round with sharp edges, and when he closed in it stopped blinking and broke into a hard left bank.

For 27 minutes it out turned and out climbed him. Twice it headed straight at him, and the first time he dove to keep from colliding while it passed over his canopy. Controllers Lloyd Jensen and H. E. Johnson watched the light from the tower through binoculars, and Dr. A. E. Cannon and his passenger Einar Nielson saw it from the Piper Cub. At about 14,000 feet Gorman's Mustang stalled while the light kept rising, until it went straight up and vanished. He told investigators he was sure there was thought behind its maneuvers.

The debate: Project Sign investigators were there within hours and even ran a Geiger counter over his plane. At first they ruled out aircraft and balloons. Then the weather bureau said it had released a lighted balloon from Fargo at 8:50 PM, and the case was closed as a balloon, with the planet Jupiter blamed for the end of the chase. A balloon drifts with the wind. This light kept coming back at him.

Can a weather balloon play chicken with a Mustang?

Source: https://www.nicap.org/reports/gorman2.htm

Two glowing objects stopped dead in front of a Japan Air Lines 747 over Alaska, and the captain said the light was so bright he felt it warm his face.
Fort Yukon to Fairbanks, Alaska. JAL Flight 1628, a 747 cargo jet at 35,000 feet, about 5:11 PM, November 17, 1986.

Captain Kenju Terauchi and his two man crew were flying a load of French wine from Paris to Tokyo by way of Iceland and Anchorage. Over the northeast corner of Alaska he noticed lights off to the left and took them for military jets, but minute after minute they kept pace with the 747. Then two of them jumped out in front of the plane, "shooting off lights," and the cockpit shined so brightly that he felt warm in the face. His weather radar showed a large green target seven or eight miles ahead.

Anchorage Center picked up an unidentified primary target near the flight, and the Air Force radar at Elmendorf reported returns too. Near Fairbanks, against the glow of the city, Terauchi saw the silhouette of something enormous, a walnut shaped craft he later said was twice the size of an aircraft carrier. He asked to turn and to descend. At 5:39 PM a controller told him military radar had an intermittent target in trail behind him and asked if he wanted fighters scrambled. He said no.

The debate: the FAA later called the extra radar target a split return from the 747 itself, a United airliner sent to look saw nothing, and skeptic Philip Klass said the crew was looking at Jupiter and Mars. Terauchi was grounded for years after he spoke to the press. Physicist Bruce Maccabee, who went through the FAA files, argued the lights were below the horizon, where no planet could be.

Would you have said no to the fighters?

Source: https://nicap.org/reports/jal1628-2.htm

Guests say small hands brush their faces in the dark at Savannah's Kehoe House, but the famous story of how those children died has no record behind it.
Savannah, Georgia. The Kehoe House on Columbia Square, built in 1892, now an inn.

William Kehoe came from Ireland as a boy, worked his way up from apprentice to owner of an iron foundry and built this towering Renaissance Revival mansion for his wife Anne and their ten children, trimmed everywhere in his own cast iron. After the family sold it around 1930, it became a boarding house and then, for decades, a funeral parlor. Football star Joe Namath owned it for a while before it became an inn.

Guests in two second floor rooms, including room 201, report being woken by what feels like the touch of small children. Others hear running feet and laughter in the halls late at night, even when no children are staying. The tour version explains it all: two Kehoe twins climbed into a chimney during hide and seek, got stuck and died, and their mother found them days later.

The debate: a Savannah Morning News search of birth, death and census records found no Kehoe twins and no chimney on any death certificate, and nine of the ten children survived infancy. A Kehoe descendant told one writer that two little girls did die young in the house, of illness, days apart. Ghost tour companies now call the chimney story debunked, and still the reports keep coming.

Would you sleep in room 201?

Source: https://www.savannahnow.com/story/entertainment/2022/03/16/savannah-georgia-ghosts-children-william-kehoe-house-inn/7004470001/

A Navy photographer filmed a dozen glowing objects over Utah, the Navy's own lab said they were not birds, and a CIA panel said seagulls.
Tremonton, Utah. About seven miles north of town, just after 11 AM, July 2, 1952.

Top 5 things to know about the Tremonton UFO film:

1) The witness: Delbert C. Newhouse was a Navy chief photographer and warrant officer with about 2,200 hours of aerial photography. He was driving his family from Washington, D.C. to Portland, Oregon when his wife pointed out a group of objects in the cloudless sky north of Tremonton, Utah.

2) The film: he pulled over, grabbed a 16mm Bell and Howell with a telephoto lens from the trunk and shot about 1,200 frames, around 75 seconds, of 10 to 14 bright objects milling across the sky. One broke away and headed the opposite direction. He later said that before he reached the camera they looked like gun-metal discs, two saucers with one upside down on the other.

3) The Navy analysis: the Navy Photo Interpretation Laboratory at Anacostia spent roughly 1,000 man-hours on it, frame by frame. Their conclusion: not birds, not balloons, not aircraft. The objects did not blink as they crossed the sky, so the lab called them self-luminous.

4) The CIA panel: in January 1953 the CIA's Robertson Panel watched the film alongside footage of seagulls in bright sun and decided the objects were most likely birds. The same panel recommended a public program of "debunking" UFOs.

5) The fight that never ended: a Douglas Aircraft analyst told Congress in 1968 that no natural explanation fully fit. The Air Force funded Condon study went to Tremonton, watched real gull flocks and called it birds. The original film still sits in the National Archives.

Navy analysts or the CIA panel, who do you believe?

Learn more: https://weightofevidence.org/cases/tremonton-1952

Twenty minutes after dark, something across the creek started throwing rocks at a father and his 14 year old son.
Weches, Texas. Big Slough in the Neches River bottoms, Davy Crockett National Forest, about 7 PM, November 14, 2026.

They had each shot a deer that day. The father packed his out first, and they came back after dark for his son's, left at the edge of the creek. While they processed it by headlamp, something threw a branch from across the creek and it smacked into the water. At the log crossing on the way out, a rock flew through the air and hit the water beside them. He yelled, thinking it was a person. No answer. A second rock splashed down. The woods were dead quiet, no owls, nothing.

For the rest of the hike something followed them just outside their lights, breaking branches and hitting trees, until they were about 200 yards from the truck. They were 28 miles of dirt road from the nearest highway. The same man says that in February 2009, about seven miles south, his headlights caught a figure covered in dark fur walking across the road. It looked at him and kept going.

The debate: nobody actually saw what threw the rocks. The investigator who interviewed him says both headlamps lit the rocks in the air, so it was no beaver tail slap, and the only other hunter near them had already driven off. Skeptics will say a person in the dark, 28 miles from pavement.

Would you have crossed that log, or turned back?

Source: https://www.bfro.net/GDB/show_report.asp?id=84780

Security police watched an unknown craft with no lights hover low over a nuclear weapons storage area, and the Air Force sent a tanker after it.
Oscoda, Michigan. Wurtsmith Air Force Base on Lake Huron, about 10:10 PM, October 30, 1975.

It started near base housing, where airmen saw what looked like the running lights of a low craft bobbing up and down. Minutes later, at 10:14, 10:20 and 10:25 PM, security police at the back gate reported an unidentified craft with no lights coming over the fence and hovering low above the Strategic Air Command weapons storage area. Then its lights came back on and it moved off to the north.

Radar Approach Control tracked a return heading southeast, out over Lake Huron. A KC-135 tanker coming home from a refueling mission was vectored after it. The crew made visual and radar contact with lit objects low over the water, and every time they tried to close, it sped away. When they swung back around one more time, a crew member said, it took off at roughly 1,000 knots. Contact was lost about 35 miles southeast of the base.

The debate: official message traffic calls it an unidentified helicopter, and no aircraft or crew was ever found or identified. It came in the middle of the 1975 wave of intrusions at northern bases like Loring in Maine and Malmstrom in Montana, documented in Air Force and NORAD records released through FOIA.

What kind of helicopter outruns a jet tanker over Lake Huron?

Source: https://www.nicap.org/reports/751030wurtsmith_rep.htm

An Air Force spy plane picked up a radar signal that ran a full circle around it at 500 mph, and then the pilots saw what was sending it.
Gulfport, Mississippi to Dallas, Texas. An RB-47 out of Forbes Air Force Base, before dawn, July 17, 1957.

A six man RB-47 crew was flying home to Kansas from a training mission over the Gulf of Mexico at 34,500 feet. Just after they crossed the coast near Gulfport, Major Frank McClure, working the electronic gear built to locate enemy radars, picked up a signal that looked exactly like a ground radar. Then it moved. The signal swept up the right side of the plane, crossed in front and slid down the left, running a ring around a bomber doing about 500 mph.

Later in the flight, pilot Major Lewis Chase saw an intensely bright light ahead of them. Ground radar near Dallas, call sign Utah, tracked an object in the same spot, and the plane's own receiver locked onto its signal. When the light blinked out, it vanished from the ground radar and the spy gear at the same moment, then came back on all of them. It stayed with the crew for more than 700 miles and an hour and a half, into Oklahoma.

The debate: Project Blue Book filed the case as an American Airlines flight. Skeptic Philip Klass argued the signals came from ground radars, the first light was a meteor and a later light was an airliner landing at Dallas. Physicist James McDonald, who interviewed the crew, called it one of the strongest cases on record, because one object showed up on eyes, radar and electronics together.

Could an airliner really fool a crew trained to hunt enemy radar?

Source: https://www.nicap.org/papers/AIAA_rep1.pdf
